- **Items or steps:** 6 ways to find which breaker feeds an outlet, in an escalation ladder from worst to best: (1) short the outlet (53 words), (2) short a cut cord plugged in first (79), (3) overload the circuit with two heaters (125), (4) inject his own signal (122), (5) a pen-style live-wire sensor, new and old (376 with its teardown), (6) a store-bought breaker finder (213, then about 630 more words taking it apart). The first three take 1:04 in all and are played as jokes; the last one gets more than half the video, because the point is what the tester is really telling you. Typical item about 125 words before the teardowns.
- **Promise devices:** the question everyone thinks they can answer (0:00); a problem-you-didn't-know ladder (each wrong way stopped with what it really does); "a better way" promised at 2:03 and paid at 8:37 (the finder finds the right breaker); a question the next block answers (9:04: what is it putting on the wire?; 9:57: how did they do it?); a guess to be checked (12:03: cut it open to see if the guess is right), paid at 13:09. The sponsor is promised for the end at 1:04.
- **Forward lines:** about 7 (2:03, 3:15, 4:29, 6:08, 7:35, 9:04, 12:03), most of them "let's" lines that start the next test. Longest gap between a forward line or payoff: about 1:35 (4:31-6:06, the sensor teardown and the breaker theory).
- **Stakes:** shock, electrocution, arc flash and a tripped building, all in the first 47 seconds and all played as comedy (cartoon superpowers, a melted outlet). After that the stakes go quiet; the danger left in the video is the presenter's own live probing (9:06), shown, not warned about. Out of proportion at the start (exaggerated for laughs), absent later.
- **Safety lines:** the "we don't do that" lines at 0:05 and 0:32 (each comes after the unsafe method has been described in enough detail to copy); a "safe current levels" line at 1:06 that introduces a deliberate overload. No power-off, verify-dead or call-an-electrician line.
- **CTA placement:** a 48-word sponsor mention at 0:47-1:04 (about 17 seconds) inside the cold open, and a 250-word sponsor read at 13:36-15:01 (about 85 seconds) after the last lesson. No subscribe, like or comment ask.
- **Ending:** the last 30 seconds of teaching (13:16-13:36) give the one practical lesson (the finder only senses where its pulse current flows, so a cord with nothing running shows nothing); then the sponsor read and a five-word thanks. No recap.
- **What sets it apart from other models of its type:**
  - The cold open acts out the wrong ways first and stops each one, so the "you've been doing it wrong" emotion lands in the first five seconds; the cost is that the unsafe methods are described before they're stopped (a viewer reports copying one).
  - It explains a tool by asking what it really tells you: the sniffer senses an electric field, so it can't tell one live breaker from another; the finder senses a pulse of current, so it only sees the circuit carrying it.
  - Comedy carries the attention (cuts, fake failures, a joke at the script), and the comments are about the presenter and the editing more than the content.

**Arc:** danger as comedy → scolded out of bad ideas → curiosity → trial and failure → it works (relief) → understanding what the tool is really telling you.

## Why it works

The audience comes for the presenter and the editing: "Mehdi is getting creative with his editing skills." (2.8K likes), "His inactivity makes me anxious but when he uploads the video I thank god that he's still with us" (1.5K likes) and "The fear that flashes across his face when the toaster and hair dryer just turn off peacefully is absolutely hilarious." (348 likes). Tradespeople learn from it too ("Electrician here! I wish Mehdi was making videos back when I was learning my trade." (353 likes)), and the practical comments add what a homeowner needs: "You plug one into the outlet then the other you sweep across the breaker box and it tells you which breaker is attached to that outlet." (72 likes), with a warning to trust a good tester ("Other brands have failed to indicate on me." (72 likes)). The opening hooks with an unsafe method stopped mid-act, then climbs a ladder of methods every 30 to 60 seconds; the second half slows into scope traces and teardowns (about 150 words a minute overall). The cost of the comic open shows in the comments: one viewer, unsure a wire was dead, says "I felt safe, but luckily decided to short live and neutral just to make sure." (18 likes), the exact move the open jokes about, and another points out the live-to-scope risk ("there goes an expensive scope by sending live voltage back down the function generator" (24 likes)). For us the topic transfers (which breaker is it, what a tester really tells you); the method of showing it does not.

## Doesn't transfer

  - [0:00] "hi everyone knows how to find the circuit breaker for a specific Outlet" (cut straight to shorting the outlet)
  - [0:27] "you might decide to cut the end of a power cord log that in first and then short out"
